card.title: How English Paragraphs Actually Work — the anatomy of connected writing

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: English paragraphs work by announcing one controlling idea early, supporting it with evidence, ANALYSING the evidence, and linking onward — held together by pronoun/synonym glue and signalled by transitions, arranged in one clear logical order.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
One paragraph = one controlling idea, announced early.
MEAL: Main idea → Evidence → Analysis → Link.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ A paragraph is 'however many sentences the teacher said'. ✅ A paragraph is one idea developed — sentences follow the idea, not a count.  ·  ❌ Starting a new paragraph whenever you like. ✅ New paragraph = new idea, new time, new place, or new speaker.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ❌ Piling transitions into every sentence ('Moreover... Furthermore... In addition...'). ✅ Use signals only where the logical relationship actually changes.  ·  ❌ Evidence without analysis ('...this shows nothing'). ✅ After every example, one sentence explains HOW it supports the main idea.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: MEAL in action: MAIN — 'Public libraries remain essential in the digital age.' EVIDENCE — 'In 2024, the Kathmandu public library recorded over 200,000 visits.' ANALYSIS — 'This shows that free access to quiet study space, not books alone, is what communities still need.' LINK — 'Libraries, in short, have changed their job, not lost it.'  ·  Cohesion chain: 'Migration has reshaped the valley. THIS FLOW of people has strained housing. SUCH PRESSURE has, in turn, driven up rents.' (pronoun + synonym glue)

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ Topic sentence at the end ('building up to the point'). ✅ In English, state the main idea first — early and explicitly.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **The big idea:** a paragraph is ONE idea, fully developed — not a fixed number of sentences. Every sentence inside exists to serve that single idea. If you start answering a new question, start a new paragraph.  ·  **The 4-part anatomy:** 1) TOPIC SENTENCE states the main idea (usually first); 2) SUPPORTING SENTENCES give reasons, facts, examples; 3) EXPLANATION/ANALYSIS links evidence back to the idea (this is the sentence weak writers skip); 4) CONCLUDING/LINK sentence rounds off or bridges to the next paragraph.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: English paragraphs lead with the conclusion (writer-responsible style).  ·  Time order in narration: 'First the alarm failed. Then the bus was missed. By the time the exam began, panic had taken over.'

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Identify topic sentence, evidence and analysis in a published article paragraph.  ·  Rewrite a jumbled 8-sentence paragraph in MEAL order and justify each move.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Unity (cut off-topic sentences) + cohesion (pronouns, synonyms, key-noun repetition) + coherence (one logical order).  ·  Transitions are traffic signals, not decoration — sparing use.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Write a 6-sentence paragraph on 'The value of morning exercise' using exactly two transitions.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **The MEAL formula for any body paragraph:** Main idea → Evidence → Analysis → Link. Say it, prove it, explain why the proof matters, connect onward. Works for essays, reports and answers alike.  ·  **UNITY test:** cover a paragraph and ask 'what is this about?' If you need two answers, split it. Every sentence that cannot be traced to the topic sentence is cut material.  ·  **COHESION — the glue devices:** pronoun reference (this policy, such measures), repeated key nouns (deliberate repetition of 'migration' anchors the paragraph), synonym chains (a student → the learner → this young person), and collocations that hold naturally in English.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **COHERENCE — logical order:** time order (first, then, finally) for narration; order of importance (most → least) for arguments; spatial order (near → far) for description; problem → cause → solution for reports. Choose ONE order per paragraph and stay in it.  ·  **TRANSITIONS — the traffic signals:** adding (moreover, in addition), contrasting (however, on the contrary), cause/effect (therefore, as a result, consequently), exemplifying (for instance, namely), sequencing (firstly, subsequently), concluding (in short, to sum up).…  ·  **WHY English paragraphs feel 'backwards' to new writers:** English is writer-responsible — the topic sentence must come EARLY and announce the point directly. Many Nepali/Asian academic styles build up to the point at the end. In English, leading with the conclusion is a feature, not rudeness.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Paragraph shape:** the classic shape is diamond — broad opening statement, narrowing specifics in the middle, slight broadening at the close. Extremely long paragraphs (250+ words) and one-sentence paragraphs both look unbalanced in essays.  ·  **Paragraph length rule of thumb:** 4-8 sentences for essays; 2-3 for news writing; 1 for notices and warnings. Length follows function.  ·  **Application to exam answers:** in long-answer questions, a new marker expects a new paragraph per point: introduction paragraph → one paragraph per argument (MEAL) → conclusion. Examiners reward visible structure as much as content.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **From reading to writing — the transfer skill:** to write better paragraphs, steal structure from what you read. Take any good article, underline topic sentences, circle transitions, and notice the evidence pattern.…
